title: Michigan House Speaker calls for end of SOAR fund and MEGA tax credits
text:
Brian Calley President and Chief Executive Officer at Small Business Association of Michigan | Official website
Brian Calley President and Chief Executive Officer at Small Business Association of Michigan | Official website
House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Township) has stated that the permanent elimination of both the Strategic Outreach and Attraction Reserve (SOAR) corporate grant program and the MEGA tax credits for large businesses is a requirement before progress can be made on economic development legislation in Michigan.
“We’re meeting, and we’re getting closer to a deal, but we’ll have to eliminate the MEGA credits and eliminate SOAR permanently – repeal it – before we’re going to move on anything,” Hall said during an episode of the MIRS Monday podcast.
Hall’s office is currently working with Senate Majority Floor Leader Sam Singh (D-East Lansing), Rep. Mark Tisdel (R-Rochester), and Rep. Mike Hoadley (R-Au Gres) to develop a “Real Jobs Tax Credit” program. This proposed initiative would allocate $50 million each year, allowing selected businesses to receive an annual payroll credit worth up to 50 percent of their income tax withholding through 2036.
Senate Democrats have expressed that companies receiving incentives should make a $100,000 “hard investment” in Michigan for every job retained within five years of accepting such incentives. Examples of these investments include purchasing from local vendors, upgrading facilities, constructing new infrastructure, supporting workforce development programs, or improving childcare access.
Hall emphasized his desire for the SOAR Fund’s permanent removal from state law. The fund previously provided significant grants intended to attract major corporate developments to Michigan until its resources were depleted following legislative budget decisions in October.
He also seeks an end to MEGA tax credits, which were notably used during Governor Jennifer Granholm’s administration as part of efforts to keep major automakers operating in Michigan during the Great Recession. Maintaining these credits remains a priority for MichAuto, an organization connected with the Detroit Regional Chamber focused on automotive and technology sectors.
Additionally, Hall indicated he wants oversight of tax credits shifted from the Michigan Economic Development Corporation (MEDC) to the state Treasurer. He said: “MEDC cannot be trusted with this. I mean, you look at what a failed record they have … every deal they’ve entered into, they spent a lot of money, and they didn’t get the jobs,” Hall stated. “It’s really important to us that small businesses can get this. If they’re creating jobs, they can get this. We want to see it be a tax credit, and we want to see it broadly applied (to) employers that pay above-average wages. We shouldn’t be paying for below-average wages.”
He referenced Ford Motor Company’s receipt of $120.3 million from SOAR funds for developing BlueOval Battery Park in Marshall as an example where offered salaries were $48,000.
Hall also acknowledged input from Singh regarding past incentive programs: “We’re listening to some of Sam’s ideas too. I mean, Sam has some very valuable experience working on this when Governor (Rick) Snyder was in office through the ‘Good Jobs,’ and so that’s really helpful to hear his perspective,” he said.
The Good Jobs program concluded in December 2019 after distributing $200 million in incentives; it provided refunds on personal income tax withholding for awarded companies such as Acrisure and Pfizer Inc.
